claim: Humans excel at selectively listening to a target speaker in background noise such as competing voices.
source: Humans excel at selectively listening to a target speaker in background noise such as competing voices.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about human auditory capabilities.

claim: The encoding of speech in the auditory cortex is modulated by selective attention.
source: While the encoding of speech in the auditory cortex is modulated by selective attention, it remains debated whether such modulation occurs already in subcortical auditory structures.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field, contrasted with the debated subcortical modulation.

claim: It remains debated whether attentional modulation occurs in subcortical auditory structures.
source: While the encoding of speech in the auditory cortex is modulated by selective attention, it remains debated whether such modulation occurs already in subcortical auditory structures.
evidence: This characterizes the current state of scientific debate in the field.

claim: Investigating the contribution of the human brainstem to attention has been hindered by the tiny amplitude of the brainstem response.
source: Investigating the contribution of the human brainstem to attention has, in particular, been hindered by the tiny amplitude of the brainstem response.
evidence: This is an inference about methodological challenges based on the physical properties of the brainstem response.

claim: Measurement of the brainstem response normally requires a large number of repetitions of the same short sound stimuli.
source: Its measurement normally requires a large number of repetitions of the same short sound stimuli, which may lead to a loss of attention and to neural adaptation.
evidence: This describes established methodological practices in the field.

claim: Large numbers of repetitions of the same short sound stimuli may lead to a loss of attention and to neural adaptation.
source: Its measurement normally requires a large number of repetitions of the same short sound stimuli, which may lead to a loss of attention and to neural adaptation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential consequences of the measurement methodology.

claim: A mathematical method was developed to measure the auditory brainstem response to running speech.
source: Here we develop a mathematical method to measure the auditory brainstem response to running speech, an acoustic stimulus that does not repeat and that has a high ecological validity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, describing the methodological contribution.

claim: Running speech is an acoustic stimulus that does not repeat and has high ecological validity.
source: Here we develop a mathematical method to measure the auditory brainstem response to running speech, an acoustic stimulus that does not repeat and that has a high ecological validity.
evidence: This characterizes the properties of running speech as a stimulus based on established knowledge.

claim: The brainstem response is consistently modulated by attention when a subject listens to one of two competing speakers.
source: We employ this method to assess the brainstem's activity when a subject listens to one of two competing speakers, and show that the brainstem response is consistently modulated by attention.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Selective attention to one of several competing acoustic signals affects the encoding of sound in the auditory cortex.
source: It is well known that selective attention to one of several competing acoustic signals affects the encoding of sound in the auditory cortex (Shinn-Cunningham, 2008; Hackley et al., 1990; Choi et al., 2013; Fritz et al., 2007b; Hillyard et al., 1973; Womelsdorf and Fries, 2007; Fritz et al., 2007a; Näätänen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Extensive auditory centrifugal pathways carry information from central to more peripheral levels of the auditory system.
source: Because extensive auditory centrifugal pathways carry information from central to more peripheral levels of the auditory system (Winer, 2006; Pickels, 1988; Song et al., 2008; Bajo et al., 2010), neural activity in the subcortical structures may contribute to attention as well.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical research.

claim: Neural activity in subcortical structures may contribute to attention.
source: Because extensive auditory centrifugal pathways carry information from central to more peripheral levels of the auditory system (Winer, 2006; Pickels, 1988; Song et al., 2008; Bajo et al., 2010), neural activity in the subcortical structures may contribute to attention as well.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical pathways and a speculation about their functional role.

claim: Previous attempts to determine attentional modulation from recording the auditory brainstem response through scalp electrodes have yielded highly inconclusive results.
source: Previous attempts to determine an attentional modulation from recording the auditory brainstem response through scalp electrodes have, however, yielded highly inconclusive results.
evidence: This characterizes the state of prior research in the field.

claim: One investigation found that selective attention alters the brainstem's response to the fundamental frequency of a speech signal.
source: In particular, one investigation found that selective attention alters the brainstem's response to the fundamental frequency of a speech signal (Galbraith et al., 1998), while another study concluded that this response is modulated in an unsystematic but subject-specific manner (Lehmann and Schönwiesner, 2014) and a third recent experiment did not find a significant attentional effect (Varghese et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Another study concluded that the brainstem's response to the fundamental frequency of speech is modulated in an unsystematic but subject-specific manner.
source: In particular, one investigation found that selective attention alters the brainstem's response to the fundamental frequency of a speech signal (Galbraith et al., 1998), while another study concluded that this response is modulated in an unsystematic but subject-specific manner (Lehmann and Schönwiesner, 2014) and a third recent experiment did not find a significant attentional effect (Varghese et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A third recent experiment did not find a significant attentional effect on the brainstem's response to the fundamental frequency of speech.
source: In particular, one investigation found that selective attention alters the brainstem's response to the fundamental frequency of a speech signal (Galbraith et al., 1998), while another study concluded that this response is modulated in an unsystematic but subject-specific manner (Lehmann and Schönwiesner, 2014) and a third recent experiment did not find a significant attentional effect (Varghese et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Results on the effects of attention on the auditory-brainstem response to short clicks or pure tones are inconclusive.
source: Results on the effects of attention on the auditory-brainstem response to short clicks or pure tones are similarly inconclusive (Brix, 1984; Gregory et al., 1989; Hoormann et al., 2000; Galbraith et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The inconsistencies in prior studies may result from the experimental limitation that the brainstem response is tiny and requires hundred- to thousandfold repetition of the same sound.
source: These inconsistencies may result from a main experimental limitation in these studies: because the brainstem response is tiny, its measurement requires hundred- to thousandfold repetition of the same sound.
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of inconsistencies in prior research.

claim: Large numbers of repetitions may lead to difficulties for subjects in sustaining selective attention.
source: The large number of repetitions may lead to difficulties for subjects in sustaining selective attention, to adaptation in the nervous system, and to a reduction in efferent feedback (Lasky, 1997; Kumar Neupane et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about potential consequences, with some citation support.

claim: Large numbers of repetitions may lead to adaptation in the nervous system.
source: The large number of repetitions may lead to difficulties for subjects in sustaining selective attention, to adaptation in the nervous system, and to a reduction in efferent feedback (Lasky, 1997; Kumar Neupane et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about potential consequences, with some citation support.

claim: Large numbers of repetitions may lead to a reduction in efferent feedback.
source: The large number of repetitions may lead to difficulties for subjects in sustaining selective attention, to adaptation in the nervous system, and to a reduction in efferent feedback (Lasky, 1997; Kumar Neupane et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about potential consequences, with some citation support.

claim: Neuronal activity in the brainstem, particularly in the inferior colliculus, can phase lock to the periodicity of voiced speech.
source: Neuronal activity in the brainstem, and in particular in the inferior colliculus, can indeed phase lock to the periodicity of voiced speech (Skoe and Kraus, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The fundamental frequency of running speech varies over time.
source: The fundamental frequency of running speech varies over time, however, compounding a direct read-out of the evoked brainstem response.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the acoustic properties of speech.

claim: The varying fundamental frequency of running speech compounds a direct read-out of the evoked brainstem response.
source: The fundamental frequency of running speech varies over time, however, compounding a direct read-out of the evoked brainstem response.
evidence: This is an inference about the methodological challenge posed by the varying fundamental frequency.

claim: Empirical mode decomposition (EMD) was employed to identify an empirical mode that oscillates at the fundamental frequency of the speech signal at each time instance.
source: To overcome this difficulty, we employed empirical mode decomposition (EMD) of the speech stimuli to identify an empirical mode that, at each time instance, oscillates at the fundamental frequency of the speech signal (Huang and Pan, 2006) (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The fundamental waveform is a nonlinear and nonstationary oscillation with a temporally-varying amplitude and frequency.
source: This mode is a nonlinear and nonstationary oscillation with a temporally-varying amplitude and frequency that we refer to as the 'fundamental waveform' of the speech stimulus (Figure 1a).
evidence: This characterizes the properties of the fundamental waveform extracted by the method, with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: The peak amplitude of the complex correlation was significantly different from the noise in fourteen out of sixteen subjects.
source: Our statistical analysis showed that the peak amplitude of the complex correlation was significantly different from the noise in fourteen out of sixteen subjects (p<0.05, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The peak of the complex correlation occurred at a mean latency of 9.3 ± 0.7 ms.
source: The peak occurred at a mean latency of 9.3 ± 0.7 ms, verifying that the measured neural response resulted from the brainstem and not from the cerebral cortex (Hashimoto et al., 1981; Picton et al., 1981).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data.

claim: The latency of 9.3 ± 0.7 ms verifies that the measured neural response resulted from the brainstem and not from the cerebral cortex.
source: The peak occurred at a mean latency of 9.3 ± 0.7 ms, verifying that the measured neural response resulted from the brainstem and not from the cerebral cortex (Hashimoto et al., 1981; Picton et al., 1981).
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured latency and supported by citations to prior research on brainstem response latencies.

claim: The latency of the brainstem response to running speech agreed with that found previously regarding the brainstem's response to short repeated speech stimuli.
source: Moreover, the latency agreed with that found previously regarding the brainstem's response to short repeated speech stimuli (Skoe and Kraus, 2010).
evidence: This compares the current findings to prior research, supported by citation.

claim: The average value of the correlation at the peak was 0.015 ± 0.003.
source: The average value of the correlation at the peak was 0.015 ± 0.003.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data.

claim: The response did not contain a stimulus artifact or a contribution from the cochlear microphonic.
source: We checked that the response did not contain a stimulus artifact or a contribution from the cochlear microphonic, and that the latency of the response was not affected by the processing of the speech signal or of the neural response (Materials and methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments described in the methods and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The latency of the response was not affected by the processing of the speech signal or of the neural response.
source: We checked that the response did not contain a stimulus artifact or a contribution from the cochlear microphonic, and that the latency of the response was not affected by the processing of the speech signal or of the neural response (Materials and methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments described in the methods and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The neural signal did not contain a measurable contribution from the cortex.
source: We also verified that the response did not contain further peaks at higher latencies, showing that the neural signal did not contain a measurable contribution from the cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of peaks at higher latencies in the experimental data.

claim: The latency of the brainstem response was unaffected by attention.
source: We found that the latency of the response was unaffected by attention: the response to the unattended speaker occurred 0.8 ± 0.5 ms later than that to the attended speaker, which was not statistically significant (p=0.2; average over the responses to the male and the female voice as well as all subjects).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: All subjects showed a larger response of the auditory brainstem to the male voice when attending rather than ignoring it.
source: In contrast, all subjects showed a larger response of the auditory brainstem, at the peak latency, to the male voice when attending rather than ignoring it (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The difference in the brainstem responses to attended versus ignored male voice was statistically significant in nine of the fourteen subjects.
source: The difference in the responses was statistically significant in nine of the fourteen subjects (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data.

claim: The brainstem's response to the attended female speaker exceeded that to the unattended female voice in all but one subject.
source: The brainstem's response to the attended female speaker similarly exceeded that to the unattended female voice in all but one subject, with eight subjects showing a statistically-significant difference (p<0.05; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Eight subjects showed a statistically-significant difference in brainstem response to attended versus ignored female voice.
source: The brainstem's response to the attended female speaker similarly exceeded that to the unattended female voice in all but one subject, with eight subjects showing a statistically-significant difference (p<0.05; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data.

claim: The ratio of the brainstem's response to attended and to ignored speech, averaged over all subjects, was 1.5 ± 0.1 for the male speaker.
source: The ratio of the brainstem's response to attended and to ignored speech, averaged over all subjects, was 1.5 ± 0.1 and 1.6 ± 0.2 for the male and for the female speaker, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data.

claim: The ratio of the brainstem's response to attended and to ignored speech, averaged over all subjects, was 1.6 ± 0.2 for the female speaker.
source: The ratio of the brainstem's response to attended and to ignored speech, averaged over all subjects, was 1.5 ± 0.1 and 1.6 ± 0.2 for the male and for the female speaker, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data.

claim: The ratio of brainstem response to attended versus ignored male voice was significantly different from unity.
source: Both ratios were significantly different from unity (p<0.001, male voice; p<0.01, female voice).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data.

claim: The ratio of brainstem response to attended versus ignored female voice was significantly different from unity.
source: Both ratios were significantly different from unity (p<0.001, male voice; p<0.01, female voice).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data.

claim: The male and the female voice elicited a comparable attentional modulation.
source: The male and the female voice elicited a comparable attentional modulation: the difference between the corresponding ratios was insignificant (p=0.7).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of the brainstem's response was significantly enhanced through attention, consistently across subjects and speakers.
source: The magnitude of the brainstem's response was hence significantly enhanced through attention, and consistently so across subjects and speakers.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The human auditory brainstem response to continuous speech is larger when attending than when ignoring a speech signal.
source: Our results show that the human auditory brainstem response to continuous speech is larger when attending than when ignoring a speech signal, and consistently so across different subjects and speakers.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The strength of the phase locking of neural activity to the pitch structure of speech is larger for an attended than for an unattended speech stream.
source: In particular, the strength of the phase locking of the neural activity to the pitch structure of speech is larger for an attended than for an unattended speech stream.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: No difference was observed in the latency of brainstem activity between attended and unattended speech.
source: In contrast, we did not observe a difference in the latency of this activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data.

claim: The fundamental waveform of speech obtained from EMD has a temporally varying frequency and amplitude and is not a simple component of Fourier analysis.
source: The fundamental waveform of speech that we have obtained from EMD has a temporally varying frequency and amplitude and is therefore not a simple component of Fourier analysis.
evidence: This characterizes the properties of the fundamental waveform based on the mathematical method used.

claim: Short-time Fourier transform and wavelet analysis suffer from an inherently limited time-frequency resolution that makes them inferior to EMD analysis.
source: While it may be obtained from short-time Fourier transform or wavelet analysis, both methods suffer from an inherently limited time-frequency resolution that makes them inferior to the EMD analysis (Huang and Pan, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on signal processing methods.

claim: The attentional modulation cannot result from a general modulation of the brainstem's activity to acoustic stimuli between the two hemispheres.
source: Because we have employed a diotic stimulus presentation in which the same acoustical stimulus was presented to each ear, the attentional modulation cannot result from a general modulation of the brainstem's activity to acoustic stimuli between the two hemispheres.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: The fundamental frequencies of the two competing speakers differ at most time points, but their spectra largely overlap.
source: Moreover, although the fundamental frequencies of the two competing speakers differ at most time points, their spectra largely overlap.
evidence: This is an inference about the acoustic properties of the stimuli.

claim: The attentional modulation cannot result from a broad-band modulation of the neural activity.
source: The attentional modulation can therefore not result from a broad-band modulation of the neural activity either.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spectral overlap of the stimuli.

claim: The attentional effect must result from a modulation of the brainstem's response to the specific pitch structure of a speech stimulus.
source: Instead, the attentional effect must result from a modulation of the brainstem's response to the specific pitch structure of a speech stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference based on ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: The brainstem response to the pitch of continuous speech can reflect a response both to the fundamental frequency of speech as well as to higher harmonics.
source: The brainstem response to the pitch of continuous speech that we have measured can reflect a response both to the fundamental frequency of speech as well as to higher harmonics.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the measured response based on established knowledge.

claim: Previous studies have found that the brainstem responds at the fundamental frequency of a speech stimulus even when that frequency itself is removed from the acoustic signal.
source: Indeed, previous studies have found that the brainstem responds at the fundamental frequency of a speech stimulus even when that frequency itself is removed from the acoustic signal (Galbraith and Doan, 1995), or when it cancels out due to presentation of stimuli with opposite polarities and averaging of the obtained responses (Aiken and Picton, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The brainstem responds at the fundamental frequency of a speech stimulus when it cancels out due to presentation of stimuli with opposite polarities and averaging of the obtained responses.
source: Indeed, previous studies have found that the brainstem responds at the fundamental frequency of a speech stimulus even when that frequency itself is removed from the acoustic signal (Galbraith and Doan, 1995), or when it cancels out due to presentation of stimuli with opposite polarities and averaging of the obtained responses (Aiken and Picton, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The attentional modulation of the brainstem response can reflect a modulation of the response to the fundamental frequency itself or to higher harmonics.
source: The attentional modulation of the brainstem response can thus reflect a modulation of the response to the fundamental frequency itself or to higher harmonics.
evidence: This is an inference about possible mechanisms underlying the observed effect.

claim: Attentional modulation of higher harmonics may depend on frequency as shown recently in recordings of otoacoustic emissions from the inner ear.
source: Moreover, attentional modulation of higher harmonics may depend on frequency as shown recently in recordings of otoacoustic emissions from the inner ear (Maison et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The attentional modulation of the brainstem's response to the pitch of a speaker may result from an enhancement of the neural response to an attended speech signal, from the suppression of the response to an ignored speech stimulus, or from both.
source: The attentional modulation of the brainstem's response to the pitch of a speaker may result from an enhancement of the neural response to an attended speech signal, from the suppression of the response to an ignored speech stimulus, or from both.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms underlying the observed effect.

claim: The response at the fundamental frequency of speech can result from multiple sites in the brainstem.
source: The response at the fundamental frequency of speech can result from multiple sites in the brainstem (Chandrasekaran and Kraus, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A single peak with a width of a few ms was observed in the correlation of the neural signal to the fundamental waveform of speech.
source: However, we observed a single peak with a width of a few ms in the correlation of the neural signal to the fundamental waveform of speech.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data.

claim: The brainstem response to running speech can only reflect neural sources whose latencies vary by a few ms or less from the peak latency.
source: The brainstem response to running speech that we have measured here can therefore only reflect neural sources whose latencies vary by a few ms or less from the peak latency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed peak width.

claim: The main neural source of the speech-evoked brainstem response may be in the inferior colliculus.
source: The neural delay of about 9 ms as well as the similarity of the speech-evoked brainstem response to the frequency-following response suggest that the main neural source may be in the inferior colliculus (Sohmer et al., 1977).
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured latency and similarity to known responses, supported by citation.

claim: The attentional effect may result from the multiple feedback loops between the inferior colliculus, the medial geniculate body and the auditory cortex.
source: The attentional effect that we have observed may then result from the multiple feedback loops between the inferior colliculus, the medial geniculate body and the auditory cortex (Huffman and Henson, 1990).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism, supported by citation to anatomical research.

claim: The study provides a mathematical methodology to analyse the brainstem response to complex, real world stimuli such as speech.
source: Our study provides a mathematical methodology to analyse the brainstem response to complex, real world stimuli such as speech.
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The method does not require artificial and repeated stimuli, fostering sustained attention and avoiding potential neural adaptation.
source: Since our method does not require artificial and repeated stimuli, it fosters sustained attention and avoids potential neural adaptation.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the method.

claim: Cochlear neuropathy or 'hidden hearing loss' alters the brainstem's activity.
source: Because the latter alters the brainstem's activity (Schaette and McAlpine, 2011; Mehraei et al., 2016), assessing the auditory brainstem response to speech as well as its modulation by attention may further clarify the origin, prevalence and consequences of such poorly understood supra-threshold hearing loss.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Assessing the auditory brainstem response to speech and its modulation by attention may clarify the origin, prevalence and consequences of cochlear neuropathy.
source: Because the latter alters the brainstem's activity (Schaette and McAlpine, 2011; Mehraei et al., 2016), assessing the auditory brainstem response to speech as well as its modulation by attention may further clarify the origin, prevalence and consequences of such poorly understood supra-threshold hearing loss.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the method.

claim: 16 healthy adult volunteers aged 18 to 32 participated in the study, eight of which were female.
source: 16 healthy adult volunteers aged 18 to 32, eight of which were female, participated in the study.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics.

claim: All subjects were native English speakers and had no history of hearing or neurological impairments.
source: All subjects were native English speakers and had no history of hearing or neurological impairments.
evidence: This describes the participant inclusion criteria.

claim: All participants had pure-tone hearing thresholds better than 20 dB hearing level in both ears at octave frequencies between 250 Hz and 8 kHz.
source: All participants had pure-tone hearing thresholds better than 20 dB hearing level in both ears at octave frequencies between 250 Hz and 8 kHz.
evidence: This describes the participant hearing characteristics.

claim: The amplitude of the brainstem response to short speech stimuli has a low-pass nature: the amplitude of the response declines with increasing frequency.
source: The auditory brainstem response to short speech stimuli has a low-pass nature: the amplitude of the response declines with increasing frequency (Musacchia et al., 2007; Skoe and Kraus, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A small but statistically significant negative correlation was found between the amplitude of the brainstem response and the fundamental frequency for the neural response to a single speaker.
source: We found a small but statistically significant negative correlation between the amplitude of the brainstem response and the fundamental frequency, both for the neural response to a single speaker as well as for the response to the attended and ignored speech signal of two competing speakers, evidencing the low-pass nature of the brainstem response (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A small but statistically significant negative correlation was found between the amplitude of the brainstem response and the fundamental frequency for the response to the attended and ignored speech signal of two competing speakers.
source: We found a small but statistically significant negative correlation between the amplitude of the brainstem response and the fundamental frequency, both for the neural response to a single speaker as well as for the response to the attended and ignored speech signal of two competing speakers, evidencing the low-pass nature of the brainstem response (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The correlations between the amplitude and the frequency did not differ significantly between the different conditions.
source: The correlations between the amplitude and the frequency did not differ significantly between the different conditions.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data.

claim: The brainstem response to short clicks in noise can have a delay that becomes longer with increasing noise level, while the amplitude of the brainstem response declines.
source: The brainstem response to short clicks in noise can have a delay that becomes longer with increasing noise level, while the amplitude of the brainstem response declines, presumably reflecting varying contributions of auditory-nerve fibers with different spontaneous rates and from different cochlear locations (Mehraei et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: No statistically-significant correlation was found between amplitude and latency for the brainstem response to continuous speech.
source: However, for the brainstem response to continuous speech that we measured here, we did not find a statistically-significant correlation between amplitude and latency (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data.

claim: Speech samples were obtained from publicly available audiobooks.
source: Samples of continuous speech from a male and a female speaker were obtained from publicly available audiobooks (https://librivox.org).
evidence: This describes the source of the experimental stimuli.

claim: All speech samples had a duration of at least two minutes and ten seconds.
source: All samples had a duration of at least two minutes and ten seconds; some were slightly longer to end upon completion of a sentence.
evidence: This describes the properties of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Speech stimuli were presented at a level of 76 dB(A) SPL.
source: Stimuli were delivered diotically through insert earphones (ER-3C, Etymotic, USA) at a level of 76 dB(A) SPL (A-weighted frequency response).
evidence: This describes the experimental parameters.

claim: All subjects reported that the stimulus level was comfortable.
source: All subjects reported that the stimulus level was comfortable.
evidence: This describes participant feedback on the experimental conditions.

claim: The impedance between each electrode and the skin was reduced to below 5 kΩ.
source: The impedance between each electrode and the skin was reduced to below 5 kΩ using abrasive electrolyte-gel (Abralyt HiCl, Easycap, Germany).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The fundamental frequency of each speech segment was interpolated through a cubic spline and varied between 100 and 300 Hz in each segment.
source: The fundamental frequency of each segment was interpolated through a cubic spline, and varied between 100 and 300 Hz in each segment.
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: The cross-correlations show that the fundamental waveform has no latency change and no phase difference with respect to the original speech stimulus.
source: The cross-correlations show that the fundamental waveform has no latency change and no phase difference with respect to the original speech stimulus.
evidence: This is a finding from control analyses.

claim: The processing of the neural signal did not induce a latency.
source: The processing of the neural signal did not induce a latency. This was confirmed by computing the cross-correlation between the processed neural response and the original signal, demonstrating a maximum correlation at zero temporal delay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a finding from control analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.
